title: Explicit Diagonal Real Missing From Any Listed Enumeration

problemStatement.formal: \forall\, f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R},\ \exists\, x \in [0,1],\ \forall\, n \in \mathbb{N},\ x \neq f(n),\ \text{where } x \text{ is the explicit diagonal real whose } n\text{-th digit differs from that of } f(n), \text{ not deduced from } \aleph_0 < \#\mathbb{R}.
problemStatement.plain: Given any sequence f(0), f(1), f(2), … of real numbers, explicitly construct a specific real x (as a definable function of f) and prove directly that x ≠ f(n) for every n, because x was built to disagree with f(n) at digit position n. This is Cantor's constructive 1891 diagonal argument, replacing the parent entry's abstract route through the cardinal inequality ℵ₀ < #ℝ.
whyMatters: The diagonal argument underlies Cantor's theorem, Turing's halting problem, Gödel's incompleteness, and Russell's paradox; a digit-level formalization exposes the reusable mechanism instead of hiding it in a cardinality lemma.
A constructive witness (an actual real x, not just an existence claim) is strictly stronger than the non-constructive cardinal statement and matches how the argument is taught.
It provides a reusable template for downstream diagonalizations in the gallery and beyond.

open: An explicit, definable map diagonalReal : (ℕ → ℝ) → ℝ producing a witness with diagonalReal f ≠ f n for all n, proven by direct digit comparison rather than via cardinality.
A clean digit-extraction and digit-comparison lemma usable for the disagreement step (n-th binary or decimal digit of a real in [0,1]), handling expansion non-uniqueness.
knownResults.goal: Define the witness x as an explicit function of the enumeration f (e.g. a bit sequence b n = if nthDigit (f n) n = 0 then 1 else 0 summed into [0,1]) and prove x ≠ f n for every n by exhibiting the differing digit, with no appeal to Cardinal.not_countable_real or #ℝ = 𝔠.
